title: Trump sons-backed Powerus merger closes, taking drone maker public
description_short: Powerus completed its merger with Trump sons-backed Aureus Greenway, becoming a Nasdaq-listed drone company.
description_medium: On October 1, 2026, Powerus and Nasdaq-listed Aureus Greenway Holdings completed their previously announced merger, with the combined company operating as Powerus Corporation and trading under ticker PUSA. The Trump brothers’ connection is through their investment in Aureus via American Ventures; company materials had identified them as investors. Their representatives described them as passive investors, and the merger itself does not establish that they held operational roles or that the company received government favors.
description_long: Powerus, the operating name of Autonomous Power Corporation, completed its merger with Nasdaq-listed Aureus Greenway Holdings on October 1, 2026. The transaction made the combined company Powerus Corporation, which continued trading on Nasdaq as PUSA. The merger had been announced in March and was completed after the parties said remaining closing conditions had been met. Company disclosures identified Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. among investors in the combined enterprise through their investment vehicle American Ventures. Reporting before the close said the brothers were passive investors in Aureus and had no operational role in the drone company; that distinction matters because the merger filing documents a corporate transaction, not their management of Powerus. Powerus described its business as defense and autonomous systems, while executives discussed adapting foreign-developed technology, including Ukrainian systems, for U.S. production. The completion is a discrete family-business event because it converted the previously announced combination into a completed publicly traded company. The sources establish the investment connection and merger, but do not show that Powerus had won a Pentagon contract by the closing date, that the Trump brothers influenced government decisions, or that the transaction involved misconduct. Those questions require separate evidence and should not be inferred from the family connection or the company’s defense ambitions.

title: Renee Good’s family sues U.S. and Trump officials over fatal ICE shooting
description_short: Renee Good’s family filed two civil suits naming the United States, the ICE agent who shot her and Trump administration officials.
description_medium: On October 1, 2026, Renee Good’s partner and brother filed two civil suits in Minnesota federal court following her January killing by an ICE agent. One names the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act; the other names the agent and current or former officials, including Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Tom Homan and Gregory Bovino, alleging excessive force and a civil-rights conspiracy. These are plaintiffs’ claims, not court findings; the White House called the suits baseless and said it would defend them.
description_long: Renee Good’s partner Becca Good and brother Brent Ganger filed two civil lawsuits on October 1, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota over Good’s January 7 fatal shooting by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Minneapolis. One complaint names the United States as the defendant under the Federal Tort Claims Act and alleges wrongful death under Minnesota law. The second names the agent, other federal agents, and current or former Trump administration officials, including Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Tom Homan and Gregory Bovino. It alleges excessive force and a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights, including claims involving Somali and Hispanic communities during Operation Metro Surge. The filing date and defendants are documented in the complaints and contemporaneous reporting. The case is a new legal event distinct from the January shooting itself, which is already represented in the frozen dataset. The complaints state the plaintiffs’ allegations; they do not establish that the shooting was unlawful, that officials conspired, or that any named defendant is liable. Reuters reported that the White House called the suits baseless and said the administration would vigorously defend itself. The reviewed sources establish the filing and the parties’ positions, but do not establish a judicial ruling on the merits or final findings about the operation, force used, or individual responsibility. Keep those procedural and evidentiary limits explicit in any later use of this record.
